pose: stout burrowing nymph with enlarged digging forelegs and wing buds
habitat: Hell Creek–Lance coastal-plain soil and litter reconstruction
blurb: The underground world cannot be reconstructed from spectacular skeletons alone. Cicadoidean insects are known from the Mesozoic, and Cretaceous relatives establish the broader lineage. CR14 therefore shows a cicada nymph as a transparent ecosystem hypothesis: biologically plausible, useful for understanding soil life, but not a claim that this exact organism has been recovered from Hell Creek.
notes:
The Hell Creek Formation preserves rivers, floodplains, soils, roots, and abundant signs of life above ground. It does not preserve every participant equally. A cicada nymph is included to make that uneven record visible. Cicadoidean insects are known from the Mesozoic, and Cretaceous relatives establish the broader lineage. That broad history makes the organism possible in a latest Cretaceous soil scene, but possibility is not the same as a local body fossil.

No described Hell Creek nymph demonstrates the exact modern body form, size, or root-feeding scene. Small or soft-bodied organisms are especially difficult to track. They may decay before burial, leave only ambiguous traces, or be preserved in deposits unlike the river sediments that dominate Hell Creek. Absence from the current fossil list can mean true absence, poor preservation, incomplete collecting, or failure to recognize a trace. The page therefore avoids a genus or species name.

The ecological role shown is feeding from plant roots while living below ground. That role is based mainly on anatomy and biology in living members of the broader group, supported by its deep evolutionary history. It is not a direct observation from 66 million years ago. Even when a lineage is old, modern behavior cannot simply be projected backward unchanged. Early members may have differed in diet, development, sociality, or habitat.

The poster’s anatomy is intentionally readable. At true scale this subject would be tiny or microscopic beside the dinosaurs, so it is enlarged in the underground cutaway. Size is stated as illustrative rather than measured from a Hell Creek specimen. Diagnostic features make the group recognizable, but some conspicuous details may be borrowed from living representatives because the local fossil does not preserve them.

Soils are ecosystems, not empty brown space. Roots change moisture and chemistry; microbes and fungi exchange nutrients; invertebrates open passages, consume material, and become prey. By including an uncertain small organism, the scene points to processes that must have occurred even when the responsible species cannot be named. The reconstruction is strongest at the level of function and weakest at the level of identity.

This distinction matters because an encyclopedia can accidentally make a picture seem more certain than the evidence behind it. A detailed illustration feels specific: every segment, strand, egg, or root contact appears chosen for a reason. Here, detail serves readability, not identification. The secure story is that Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystems contained complex communities of small organisms and that cicadas had an evolutionary history relevant to this interval. The insecure story would be that the exact individual drawn here occupied this exact patch of Hell Creek soil. We accept the first and explicitly decline the second.

Living cicadas show what such organisms can do, not exactly what this Cretaceous form did. They are comparison points for explaining anatomy and ecology. Evolution over tens of millions of years prevents us from treating a living species as a frozen fossil. The “Still With Us Today” connection is continuity of a broad lineage or role, never a claim of unchanged species.

In the poster, CR14 is a deliberate evidence lesson. Its presence says that a living floodplain required small actors as well as famous vertebrates. Its label remains indeterminate, its confidence is low, and the page states the missing local evidence plainly. The pose, color, scale, exact location, and interaction with surrounding soil are artistic. If a future Hell Creek fossil narrows the identification, the digital page can be revised while the printed scene remains honestly labeled.

Future evidence could strengthen or remove this entry. A diagnostic body fossil, amber inclusion, eggshell association, trace fossil with an identifiable maker, or microscopic root preservation would each answer different questions. Until then, the confidence badge and indeterminate label carry real scientific meaning: the page teaches not only what ancient life may have contained, but how researchers know when a reconstruction has reached beyond the preserved record.
funFacts: The preservation filter — No described Hell Creek nymph demonstrates the exact modern body form, size, or root-feeding scene. Tiny and soft organisms are often missing even from rich fossil ecosystems.
A group is not a species — The label is deliberately indeterminate. It identifies a broad biological model without inventing a fossil species name.
The poster enlarges it — The underground figure is made visible for teaching and is not drawn at the same scale as the large surface animals.
Function is firmer than identity — Cicadoidean insects are known from the Mesozoic, and Cretaceous relatives establish the broader lineage; the exact Hell Creek participant remains unresolved.
survivor: Living cicadas remain part of soils and food webs today, offering a living comparison for the role shown here. They do not prove that the Hell Creek organism had the same species, size, color, behavior, or anatomy. The connection is deliberately broad: an old lineage and an ecological process that survived while particular forms changed. Modern biology helps us ask better questions of the fossil record; it should not be used to fill every gap as though evolution had paused.
distribution: This entry does not map a named fossil species. Its broad lineage is documented from Cretaceous or older deposits, while the poster setting is the latest Cretaceous Hell Creek–Lance coastal plain of western North America. No described Hell Creek nymph demonstrates the exact modern body form, size, or root-feeding scene. The illustrated location among roots is an ecosystem reconstruction based on plausible habitat and modern functional comparison. It must not be converted into a locality point, species range, or claim of a body fossil from the poster site.

directEvidence: Mesozoic fossils establish cicadoidean lineages before the end of the Cretaceous.
Modern cicada nymphs have digging forelegs and feed underground from plant xylem.
The Hell Creek individual, size, host root, and precise anatomy are not directly fossilized.
supportedInference: A member of the broad group could plausibly have occupied a latest Cretaceous soil ecosystem.
The ecological role shown is inferred from living biology and evolutionary continuity.
Hell Creek soils provided a possible setting for the interaction.

The pose, behavior, and placement beside a particular root.
